papers.title: A Local Enrichment Computational Framework to Identify Disease-Enriched Physical Activity Patterns
papers.abstract: Wearable accelerometers enable continuous monitoring of physical activity (PA), yet conventional summary measures and population-wide clustering approaches may overlook disease-associated behavioral heterogeneity. Here we introduce LocPA, a computational framework that identifies disease-enriched PA patterns through confounder-adjusted activity profiling, similarity network construction, local disease-enrichment testing and community detection. Applying LocPA to 24-hour accelerometry profiles from the UK Biobank, we identified two recurring PA phenotypes across six diseases spanning cardiometabolic, neurological, psychiatric, renal and cardiovascular conditions: a low-activity phenotype characterized by reduced daytime activity and a sleep-disrupted phenotype characterized by reduced daytime and elevated nocturnal activity. In hypertension and diabetes, the sleep-disrupted phenotype was associated with greater disease burden and less favorable clinical and metabolic profiles, differences not consistently captured by conventional PA summary measures. LocPA also identified disease-specific temporal patterns, particularly in Parkinsons disease. Analyses in an independent National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey cohort supported the recurrence of hypertension- and diabetes-enriched patterns across populations and accelerometry measurements. LocPA provides a flexible, disease-driven approach for uncovering clinically relevant temporal PA patterns, with potential applications in disease risk characterization and personalized behavioral interventions.

papers.title: Bern Sleep-Wake Registry: temporal extraction of comorbidities from unstructured clinical text using a large language model
papers.abstract: Introduction Large language models (LLMs) may enable the extraction of clinically relevant information from unstructured electronic health records, but most previous work focused on identifying diagnoses without preserving their temporal context. We evaluated the ability of an LLM to extract diagnoses and associated dates from longitudinal clinical reports. Methods In an observational study using the Bern Sleep-Wake Registry, diagnostic annotations from 248 patients comprising 2343 clinical entries were analyzed. Six common comorbidity groups, subdivided into 32 hierarchical diagnostic categories, were evaluated. Using gpt-oss-20b, we extracted diagnosis presence, the number of diagnostic instances, and dates per instance. A reference standard was established through independent review by two physicians, with disagreements adjudicated by a third physician. LLM performance was assessed using diagnostic classification and temporal agreement. Direct annotation costs were compared. Results At the patient level, the LLM achieved an overall F1 score of 0.88 for diagnosis presence and 0.96 for the presence of a reported date. For the earliest reported diagnosis date, agreement with the reference standard was 86.73% at the day level. When considering the cumulative set of dates for each diagnosis, date recall was 87.63%, the extra-date rate was 20.88%, and full agreement was achieved in 58.19% of cases. Human annotators showed substantial disagreement in temporal annotation, with a date recall of 75.49%, an extra-date rate of 17.89%, and full agreement in 58.64% of cases. LLM-based extraction reduced direct annotation costs by 94.65%. Conclusions LLMs can extract diagnoses and their dates from heterogeneous clinical text with high agreement with an adjudicated reference standard. These findings support the scalable use of LLMs for longitudinal clinical registries.

papers.title: Trajectories and characteristics of pain in the first year after spinal cord injury: a TRACK-SCI study
papers.abstract: Chronic pain affects most individuals with spinal cord injury (SCI) and frequently impairs daily function, and nearly half experience neuropathic pain. Neuropathic pain is commonly thought to develop months after injury and to persist once established. These views rest on classifying each patient as having neuropathic pain or not, although patients often report several pains. The same binary label is the usual target of prognostic and biomarker studies that aim to predict life-limiting pain. We tracked up to three of the worst pains per interview from injury to one year in 140 TRACK-SCI participants, using the DN4 interview (DN4i, threshold 3). Within three days of injury, half of all pain areas and three quarters of participants met the threshold, and pain-area prevalence changed little over the year. Individual pains, however, often changed. Only a third remained above the threshold throughout, one third resolved or fluctuated, and pains in the same person often followed different courses. At more than half of interviews with several pains, one pain met the threshold while another did not, so that the patient's classification depended on the pain considered. We therefore derived a threshold-free Pain Composite Score from the DN4i items and pain intensity. The items formed a single dimension, and the composite was associated with sleep and mood interference whereas the binary classification was not. Neuropathic pain after SCI thus appears early, does not invariably persist, and differs between a person's pains, and graded pain-level measures may offer a more stable target for predicting life-limiting pain.

papers.title: Automated Sleep Staging Performance Across Two Experimental Sleep Manipulation Protocols in Adolescents.
papers.abstract: Automated sleep staging algorithms improve the scalability of polysomnography analysis in adolescent research but are primarily validated in undisturbed, single-night sleep recordings. It remains unclear whether these algorithms maintain performance when sleep architecture is experimentally manipulated. This study evaluated the validity of two popular automated sleep staging approaches across two distinct sleep manipulation paradigms in adolescents: a sleep restriction protocol (N=43, mean age [SD]=13.37[1.06] years; four nights including two sleep extension [10hr] and two restriction [4hr] nights) and a slow-wave sleep deprivation (SWSD) protocol (N=18, mean age [SD]=17.17[1.79] years; baseline, SWSD, and recovery nights). Automated sleep staging was performed using the POPulation-level Sleep Stager (POPS), the Yet Another Spindle Algorithm (YASA), and combined POPS+YASA. Manual polysomnography scoring by experienced sleep technicians served as the reference standard. Agreement was assessed using Cohen's k, and stage-specific performance was evaluated using F1 scores and confusion matrices. Mixed-effects models tested differences in overall and stage-specific agreement across nights. All staging approaches demonstrated moderate-to-substantial agreement with manual scoring across manipulated sleep conditions (k range; range=0.53-0.76). In the sleep restriction study, agreement was lower in restricted versus extended sleep (P<0.05), and agreement declined across restriction nights, with poorer Wake, N1, and N2 classification, while N3 remained preserved. In the SWSD study, overall agreement was lower on the SWSD night, with poorer N3 classification while other stages were preserved. Automated sleep staging performance may be less consistent in adolescents when sleep is curtailed or fragmented; future studies should develop and validate these algorithms under multiple sleep conditions.

papers.title: Beyond reduced alpha power: a weaker temporal link between alpha and other brain rhythms in Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: Background: Reduced alpha power is among the most consistently reported resting electroencephalography (EEG) features of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, alpha activity also interacts with other rhythms over time, a dynamic aspect that power measures do not capture. Whether AD weakens this temporal interaction, and whether such a change carries information beyond reduced alpha power, remains unclear. Methods: We analyzed public eyes-closed resting EEG from 29 healthy controls (HC), 36 patients with AD and 23 with frontotemporal dementia (FTD). After separating periodic from aperiodic activity, we tracked the aperiodic exponent and periodic theta, alpha, beta and gamma activity in consecutive 1-s windows. A vector autoregressive model predicted these five measures from the preceding window. Alpha's predictive contribution (G) was the increase in prediction error for theta, beta and gamma when the model was refitted without alpha as a predictor, with training and testing on separate time blocks of each recording. AD-HC differences were adjusted for age and sex, then for alpha expression (periodic alpha power) and signal quality (dynamic range and spatial reliability), with alpha self-persistence (alpha's carry-over between windows) as a benchmark. We also tested whether expression and G each added information about AD beyond the other. An exploratory Jansen-Rit-family circuit model examined whether expression and G can change partly independently. Results: G was lower in AD than in HC (adjusted difference in 10^3G, -3.19; 95% confidence interval -5.25 to -1.13; p = 0.0035), with a consistent direction across sensitivity analyses. Adjustment for alpha expression and signal quality retained 75.8% of this difference but only 4.4% of the self-persistence difference. Expression and G each added information beyond the other (Holm-adjusted p = 0.012 for both). FTD contrasts were inconclusive. In the circuit model, reducing local recurrent excitation lowered alpha expression without an estimated decrease in G, whereas reducing downstream input lowered G with a smaller change in expression. Conclusions: At the group level, the resting alpha abnormality in AD comprises two partly nonredundant dimensions: reduced expression and a weaker temporal link between alpha and subsequent multi-rhythm activity. Quantifying this temporal link may complement conventional spectral markers of AD.
